name: Electric Bicycle
description: A bicycle with fully operable pedals and an electric motor of no more than 750 watts, in one of three classes: Class 1 and Class 3 pedal-assist up to 20 and 28 mph, and Class 2 motor-propelled up to 20 mph.

restrictions.rule: A bicycle with fully operable pedals and a motor of no more than 750 watts
restrictions.citation: Hawaii Revised Statutes §§249-1, 291C-1, as amended by HB 2021 (2026)

restrictions.rule: Class 1 assists only while the rider pedals and stops at 20 mph; Class 2's motor can propel it alone, up to 20 mph; Class 3 assists only while pedaling, stops at 28 mph and must have a speedometer
restrictions.citation: Hawaii Revised Statutes §291C-1, as amended by HB 2021 (2026)

restrictions.rule: A device with a motor over 750 watts that can exceed 28 mph is a high-speed electric device, not an electric bicycle, and can't be ridden on any public road, bike lane, path or sidewalk
A road-legal two- or three-wheeler whose electric motor can exceed 28 mph is an electric motorcycle, licensed, registered and insured like a motorcycle and barred from bike lanes and paths
Riders under 16 may ride a Class 2 or Class 3 only under the direct supervision of a parent, guardian or adult 18 or older
Riders under 18, and children in an attached seat or towed trailer, must wear a bicycle helmet
Must be registered with the county director of finance for a one-time $30 fee before riding it on a public road, sidewalk or bicycle facility; an unregistered one can be cited or impounded
No insurance required for a road-legal, registered and classified electric bicycle
Must be ridden seated, facing forward, with all wheels on the ground: no wheelies, stunts, or standing on the seat or riding on the handlebars
May be ridden on a sidewalk at no more than 10 mph, except in business districts or where a county ordinance bans it
Counties may restrict it further on sidewalks and post bike lanes and paths to keep motor-equipped bicycles off them

Carries a permanent label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage, which no one may alter, deface or remove; the requirement starts 120 days after Act 259's enactment, or sooner once rules are adopted

Sellers, including online and third-party platforms delivering to Hawaii, must tell the buyer in writing whether it is legal on public roads, sidewalks and bike lanes, with its registration, equipment, helmet and age rules; distributors post a point-of-sale sign that e-bike sales and riding are regulated and give buyers a pamphlet of the state laws, and the Department of Transportation may fine each violation up to $500
Police and county finance officers may seize one that isn't road-legal, or that doesn't meet its class, label, equipment or operating rules
restrictions.citation: Hawaii Revised Statutes §249-15, as amended by HB 2021 (2026)
